newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan war speads to Kabul skies.
newsitem.headline: Afghan war speads to Kabul skies.

text.p: Aircraft apparently belonging to the anti-Taleban alliance swept over Kabul twice on a moonlit night and again early on Sunday, dropping bombs on the airport and setting off furious barrages of anti-aircaft fire.
Witnesses said the first plane, which screamed low over the city just before 9 p.m. (1630 GMT), appeared to have dropped two bombs close to the airport on the northeast fringe of the Afghan capital.
A second appeared about three hours later and two huge explosions rocked central Kabul.
Witnesses said the bombs hit a park, shredding trees and shattering glass in some 40 nearby shops, but apparently wounding no one.

Early on Sunday morning, another plane roared over the city and aimed two bombs at the airport, which is used for both civilian and military traffic. Witnesses said it was not clear whether they caused significant damage.
They were the first air raids on Kabul since the purist Islamic Taleban took the capital a month ago.
Militia fighters fired anti-aircraft guns, heavy machine guns and at least one rocket at the intruders, but there was no sign that they hit anything.

It was not known whether the plane, or planes, belonged to northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum, who is known to have a small air force, or ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, who is believed to still have a few aircraft.
The two joined forces formally two weeks ago after two years of bitter estrangement and Dostum sent tanks, artillery and men to Masood's front line on the plain north of Kabul.
Last week the Taleban started using two combat aircraft -- a MiG-25 and a Sukhoi -- to help hold their lines in a hilly zone some 25-30 km (15-18 miles) north of Kabul.
In one raid a Taleban bomb killed at least 14 civilians in the front-line village of Kalakan.

The air raids were the latest evidence that the war between the Taleban, who now control three-quarters of Afghanistan, and the northern alliance is moving into new fields and that hopes of a ceasefire are dead.

The front lines north of Kabul have been static for a week, despite several attempts by Masood to force a breakthrough on to dusty rolling land that runs to the pass leading down into the city he left without a fight.
The Taleban have been noticeably more confident after holding Masood, who has been fighting with the artillery support of Dostum, but it has not been clear whether Uzbek troops have been involved.
On Thursday, the Taleban signalled an end to any lingering hopes of a ceasefire by attacking Dostum directly in the remote northwestern province of Badghis.
The Taleban said they had taken the province and pushed into neighbouring Faryab province. If they took that, they could then threaten Dostum's capital of Mazar-i-Sharif.
On Saturday a Masood spokesman implicitly denied the loss of Badghis, saying fighting was continuing and mostly involved infantry and armoured vehicles.
There have been no reliable independent reports from the area, but Afghan watchers said the attack there suggested considerable confidence on the part of the Taleban.
